entries.title: Rapper BloodHound Q50, 22, fatally shot in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County medical examiner's office identified a 22-year-old man who was fatally shot Sunday morning in Fuller Park as Mikquale Cooper of Chicago.</p><p>A manager with AMF Music Group confirmed Cooper was the rap artist who performed as BloodHound Q50.</p><p>Chicago police said Cooper was in a car around 4 a.m. in the 4200 block of South Wentworth Avenue when two cars pulled up alongside and several people in both vehicles fired shots at him, according to police.</p><p>Cooper was shot in the chest and shoulder.</p><p>He was treated by Chicago Fire Department personnel and was pronounced dead at the scene, police said.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Bears' next opponent: Vikings score 29 straight points to beat Packers 39-22
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Carson Wentz has had little time to practice with Minnesota's voluminous playbook, a late arrival to the team last season who returned this year in more of a mentor role as Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy competed for the starting quarterback job in training camp.</p><p>The Vikings brought the 11th-year veteran back for emergencies like these.</p><p>Wentz came in after Murray's first-quarter concussion in his Minnesota debut and led a spirited comeback against the rival Green Bay Packers, as the Vikings scored 29 straight points to close a 39-22 victory to open the season on Sunday.</p><p>"That's why he's here," coach Kevin O'Connell said. "For him to come in and do what he did and just be part of that calming presence that allowed our team to continue playing, I can't say enough about him."</p><p>Wentz had two touchdown passes to Justin Jefferson, matching the two-time All-Pro's 2025 season total, and the pair connected on a 2-point conversion when the Vikings took their first lead at 25-22 with 6:37 remaining. Green Bay extended the drive three times with crushing defensive penalties.</p><p>"Football is a funny game," Wentz said, "but it's fun to be on this side of it."</p><p>Jordan Love, who had been brilliant against a relentlessly blitzing defense, wilted along with the rest of the team by losing a fumble on a sack and throwing an interception deep in Packers territory.</p><p>Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason each had rushing touchdowns and T.J. Hockenson caught one of the three scores thrown on a turnover-free afternoon by Wentz, who was appointed the backup to Murray ahead of the 2024 first-round draft pick McCarthy for his considerable edge in experience.</p><p>Wentz went helped the Vikings convert eight of 15 third downs and posted a 123.5 passer rating in another memorable comeback among many in five seasons under O'Connell, who has yet to win a playoff game.</p><p>"This one will stick with me for a long time," O'Connell said.</p><p>Momentum shifted when the Packers were stopped on fourth-and-1.</p><p>Love finished 21 for 42 for 387 yards and two first-half touchdowns to Christian Watson, but the two late turnovers and a 3-for-12 conversion rate on third downs loomed large as the Packers picked right up where they left off with a five-game losing streak that ended last season.</p><p>The Packers lost four times after leading in the second half by at least two possessions, including their wild card playoff collapse against the Bears, who outscored the Packers 25-6 in the fourth quarter of that game.</p><p>Green Bay coach Matt LaFleur might have mistakenly triggered this meltdown with his decision to take rookie Trey Smack's field goal off the board to set up a fourth-and-1 on an offside penalty. Love was stuffed at the line with a five-point lead, and the Vikings went the other way for the go-ahead score by Jones, the former Packers favorite who had yet to reach the end zone against his former team.</p><p>The Packers actually four defensive penalties on that drive, starting with a seemingly innocent encroachment call on Jonathan Ford.</p><p>Javon Bullard, whose injurious hit on Murray was flagged, was called for illegal contact to negate a third-down sack. Rookie Chris McClellan was penalized for a late hit on Wentz to wipe out a third-down incompletion. Then Xavier McKinney's defensive holding call erased an end-zone interception by Evan Williams, and Jones scored on the next play.</p><p>Though the penalties on McClellan and McKinney in particular were contested by the Packers, they had only themselves to blame for this collapse.</p><p>"Momentum is a strong thing," Watson said, "and we didn't respond."</p><h3>Injury report</h3><h3></h3><p>Murray seemed to be doing well after the game, O'Connell said, but the timetable for his return was unknown. ... Packers LG Aaron Banks (knee) was inactive, giving Donovan Jennings his first career start.</p><h3>Up next</h3><h3></h3><p><b>Packers:</b> at New York Jets on Sept. 20.</p><p><b>Vikings:</b> vs. the Bears at Soldier Field on Sept. 20.<br></p>

entries.title: A year after Operation Midway Blitz, Chicago celebrates 'strength' at the Mexican Independence Day Parade
entries.summary: <p>A year after immigration threats tempered many of Chicago's Mexican Independence Day celebrations, this year's parade aimed to bring back the full 400,000 spectators it expects to garner.</p><p>Last year's parade <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/05/mexican-independence-day-parade-little-village-immigration-ice-threat" target="_blank" >continued as planned</a>, despite fears of immigration raids during <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>, President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement campaign targeting Chicago. But, leaders encouraged would-be attendees to do what they felt would be safest and view the parade from home, if they desired.</p><p>This year, the theme of the 55th annual event was "United We Ride: Stronger Than Ever." Held by the Little Village Chamber of Commerce, organizers said the event is one of the largest parades in the Midwest and serves as a cultural celebration and an economic driver for local businesses.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f90000" name="image-f90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/44fca55/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2192851/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c99fca9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6048x3394+0+319/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F75%2F1df6f08c48e79b7fc74e8d2f1401%2Fmexicandayparade-260914-33-flag.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Participants carry large Mexican flags down 26th Street during the 55th Annual Mexican Independence Day Parade in Chicago's Little Village neighborhood on Sunday, September 13, 2026. entries.title: Man seriously wounded in South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man whose age was not immediately available was in serious condition Sunday after he was shot in the stomach in the South Shore neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Police said the man had been involved in a verbal argument with an unknown assailant who fired shots along the 2900 block of East 77th Street at about 3:15 p.m.</p><p>The victim was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was initially reported in serious condition, police said.</p><p>Area Two detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Fire fall to Revolution 2-1 at Soldier Field
entries.summary: <p>Dor Turgeman had a first-half goal and a second-half assist, Peyton Miller scored in his 50th MLS start and the New England Revolution beat the Chicago Fire 2-1 on Sunday at Soldier Field.</p><p>New England (13-8-4) moved into sole possession of third place in the Eastern Conference with 43 points, 11 behind first-place Nashville.</p><p>Chicago (11-7-6) was coming off a 1-1 draw against Inter Miami CF in front of a club-record 63,094 fans.</p><p>Turgeman opened the scoring in the 39th minute. He won a one-one-one race with Chicago defender Sam Rogers for a long ball and sent a shot past a diving Chris Brady.</p><p>Miller made it 2-0 lead in the 47th when he was left wide open at the far post to tap in a pass across the goal by Turgeman.</p><p>Maren Haile-Selassie guided in a shot into the far corner from the top of the 18-yard box in the 62nd to pull Chicago within 2-1.</p><p>New England coach Marko Mitrović returned to Chicago to face his former club after serving as an assistant coach with the Fire from 2016-19.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>New England: Hosts Orlando on Saturday.</p><p>Chicago: At Nashville on Saturday.</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Dear Abby: Grandmas go head-to-head over nickname used by child
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My grandson is 2 and has started to call me "Mimi." The problem is that his other grandmother chose Mimi for herself. My daughter-in-law is annoyed and does not want him calling me Mimi. She also doesn't want me to be called Mom-Mom because he calls her Ma-Ma. Am I wrong to be upset? I've been an active caregiver in this child's life since his birth. His other Mimi does not live nearby and makes no effort to be in her grandchild's life — not even by phone. She just uses the term Mimi to sound good to her Facebook friends.</p><p>I know this is silly, but is it wrong for me to be upset? He needs something simple to call me when we go to playgrounds and can't find me. I feel that he can have two Mimis. I grew up with two moms. — <i>NICKNAME IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR NICKNAME:</b> More than one Mimi could be confusing. The most important thing is your relationship with your grandchild, not who has dibs on a certain name. I suggest you let the other grandmother claim "Mimi" while you collaborate with the little boy on a new nickname for you. If he takes part in the decision, it will be easier for him to remember and a lot more special.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been married for 12 years and have two stepchildren. My 37-year-old stepson is the challenging one. He's the biggest cheapskate I have come across in my entire life. Although he earns a good living in his profession, he rarely picks up the tab when we go out to dinner or drinks, and he almost never picks up his own tab, either. He seems to expect that we, as parents, are obligated to take care of his expenses.</p><p>My wife has recently begun picking up his portion, but I find it infuriating that he makes no gesture at all to pay his own way. Should I just let it go and continue letting his mother pick up his portion (from her separate account), while I continue to stress about it? — <i>CHEAPSKATE'S STEPDAD IN NEW MEXICO</i></p><p><b>DEAR STEPDAD:</b> Has your wife asked you not to talk with her son about this? If she hasn't, have you told him he's too old for Mom to constantly pay his tab, particularly in light of the fact that he's a fully employed adult? (One would think he should have volunteered, if only occasionally.) I will assume you have told your wife how you feel about this, that when she picks up her son's portion it makes you lose your appetite. Start there, but if she continues, remember that that money is hers, and how she chooses to spend it is her business.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> The manager of the dining room in my senior living center has a habit of shaking hands with residents at their tables. To avoid his hand, I often say my hand is wet or greasy. How can I best decline his unsanitary effort? — <i>HEALTHY HANDS IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEALTHY:</b> The manager wants to appear friendly and welcoming. Because you prefer not to shake hands while dining, simply tell him as much. If you say it with a polite smile and a good-natured tone, it shouldn't cause embarrassment.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: State's attorney's proposed pretrial changes undermine justice
entries.summary: <p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke’s recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountystatesattorney.org/news/icymi-states-attorney-burke-pens-chicago-tribune-op-ed-electronic-monitoring-system-broken" target="_blank" >calls</a> for legislative changes to how pretrial release works — and criticism of the judges making those decisions — is deeply disappointing.</p><p>The presumption of innocence and due process are foundational principles of our legal system, so it is troubling to see O’Neill Burke, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and judge, attacking these concepts and the judiciary's independent decision-making.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/11/19/23960567/pretrial-fairness-act-illinois-criminal-justice-equity-lisel-petis" >Pretrial Fairness Act</a> requires judges to consider the unique facts of each case and person when deciding whether someone should be detained.</p><p>O’Neill Burke says she supports the law’s removal of the role of money in those decisions, but then suggests that the seriousness of the allegation alone should require detention.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d50000" name="module-d50000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Judges already account for the severity of the allegations when determining pretrial release, and requiring incarceration based on the charge alone would be both unconstitutional and a disaster in a county where 1 out of 3 people charged with a felony is ultimately found not guilty or has their case dismissed.</p><p>Take our client Vanessa Sanders, who was charged with first-degree murder after she stabbed her abusive boyfriend in a clear act of self-defense.</p><p>Citing the prosecution, media initially covered Vanessa as a woman who killed her boyfriend because <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/6/24/18442390/prosecutors-woman-fatally-stabbed-man-for-pulling-her-hair" >“he pulled her hair.”</a> In reality, Sanders had her hair ripped from her scalp before she defended herself.</p><p>Like the vast majority of people facing a murder charge, Vanessa was detained. She spent over seven years in jail awaiting trial at the snail’s pace of the Cook County courts. When finally released on electronic monitoring, Vanessa was present for every court hearing, hoping to clear her name. Earlier this summer, it took a jury one hour to find her <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/24/prosecutors-expected-to-offer-new-deal-to-woman-accused-of-killing-boyfriend-as-trial-kicks-off" >not guilty</a>. But a person who is acquitted never gets that time back and never gets restitution for the years of freedom they were denied.</p><p>When the question is asked, “Why are some people charged with serious offenses like murder sometimes released pretrial?” the answer is often that their cases look like Vanessa’s.</p><p>Vanessa should never have been jailed.</p><p>Despite the seriousness of her charge, the fact that Vanessa had a strong self-defense claim and the deceased was an intimate partner with a history of physical abuse shows she was not a danger to the public.</p><p>Clearly, prosecutors don’t always get it right when it comes to charging.</p><p>Giving the state’s attorney the power to effectively determine who gets locked up simply by choosing what charges to file doesn’t just undermine judicial discretion, it risks rigging the system so prosecutors control both the accusation and its consequence.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div There is an American flag to the left. Behind the woman is a flag that reads, "Cook County State’s Attorney."" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f08bdd3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4953x2780+0+261/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F60%2Fbc%2Fdefd3a2a4eee92257fe161051d6a%2Feobcharges-081425-19.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7b3fd3f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4953x2780+0+261/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F60%2Fbc%2Fdefd3a2a4eee92257fe161051d6a%2Feobcharges-081425-19.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f08bdd3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4953x2780+0+261/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F60%2Fbc%2Fdefd3a2a4eee92257fe161051d6a%2Feobcharges-081425-19.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Our pretrial system, where judges make decisions based on the evidence and strength of a case after listening to prosecution and defense arguments, accounts for the fact that these are only allegations.</p><p>The prosecution’s detention requests are approved twice as often as they are denied. O’Neill Burke's blanket policies to seek detention in many cases have caused the jail population to be higher now than before the Pretrial Fairness Act took effect. That’s apparently not enough detention, even though crime rates are at historic lows and have consistently fallen over time, despite an uptick during COVID-19.</p><p>It is also worth noting an area where O’Neill Burke has done almost nothing to hold people who commit violence against the public responsible for their actions: employees of the federal government.</p><p>The sole prosecution O’Neill Burke has undertaken since <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/08/how-operation-midway-blitz-played-out" >Operation Midway Blitz</a> is a misdemeanor charge against an off-duty U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/12/ice-adam-saracco-attack-robert-held" >attacked a senior citizen</a> filming him at a gas station — despite the option to charge a felony based on the victim’s age. The state’s reasoning was simply that a misdemeanor was “more appropriate.” In contrast, our clients who are not law enforcement officers are consistently charged with the highest possible offense.</p><p>Notably, O’Neill Burke also didn’t complain about the lack of pretrial detention in that case or demand incarceration for the agent as part of his guilty plea.</p><p>And while the state’s attorney has not acted on the staggering violence ICE has directed at community members responding to the detention of their neighbors for civil immigration violations, she has prosecuted <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/02/26/why-is-the-cook-county-states-attorney-prosecuting-nonviolent-ice-protesters/" target="_blank" >more than 100 people</a> for protesting that violence.</p><p>O’Neill Burke has supported important reforms, but her actions over the last 18 months have raised questions about the consistency of her commitment to fairness in the criminal process. </p><p>The presumption of innocence requires individualized decisions regarding pretrial release, and law enforcement officers deserve to be held to a higher standard — not let off easier than the public.</p><p><i>Sharone R. Mitchell Jr. is the Cook County public defender.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: New report finds 35% of Chicago households don’t have sufficient food
entries.summary: <p>An estimated 35% of households in Chicago face some form of food insecurity, according to a report published Monday by the Greater Chicago Food Depository.</p><p>The depository, which supplies food to hundreds of food pantries across Cook County, partnered for the first time with NORC at the University of Chicago to release “Hunger in Chicago Report,” detailing which communities and types of households face some level of food insecurity, which is defined as experiencing disrupted eating patterns or reduced food.</p><p>Chicago residents who participated in the survey this summer were asked a series of questions, such as if household members in the past 30 days had either skipped meals or reduced portions because there wasn’t enough money to buy food.</p><p>The report released Monday indicates food insecurity is more widespread than what previous reports had indicated. In 2024, about 13% of households in Illinois were experiencing food insecurity and about 24% were marginally food insecure, according to an analysis of data from the <a class="Link" href="https://ukcpr.uky.edu/resources" target="_blank" ><u>University of Kentucky Center for Poverty Research</u></a>.</p><p>Kate Maehr, chief executive officer for the Greater Chicago Food Depository, said the food insecurity people are experiencing is driven by inflation driving up grocery prices and families still recovering from changes to the economy since the COVID-19 pandemic.</p><p>“The data is so stark, and the stakes are so high,” Maehr said. “This is a basic, moral issue. I believe that food is a basic human right, and more than a third of the households in our great city are struggling with access to something as basic as food.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-530000" name="html-embed-module-530000"></a><div style="min-height:306px" id="datawrapper-vis-OtYVx"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OtYVx/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-OtYVx"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OtYVx/full.png" alt="Food insecurity by population type (Stacked Bars)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The greater need for food comes amid changes to the largest food assistance program, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. SNAP has undergone <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/04/30/snap-food-assistance-cutoffs-begin-friday-in-illinois-what-you-need-to-know" target="_blank" ><u>expanded work requirements</u></a> for participants and will dramatically shift program costs to states as part of President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending plan often referred to as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was signed into law last year.</p><p>Already in Illinois, participation in the federally-funded food assistance program has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/27/illinois-sees-16-drop-in-snap-enrollment-one-year-after-food-program-overhaul" target="_blank" ><u>fallen by 16% compared to 2025</u></a>, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. As of June, the number of people receiving SNAP benefits dropped to nearly 1.6 million people — the lowest number of people receiving food assistance in the state since 2009.</p><p>Maehr described the changes as “the rug being pulled out from under the feet of families that were vulnerable, and it took away this critical resource for so many people.”</p><p>Food insecurity is particularly pronounced on the South Side, where 51% of residents surveyed indicated they either had very low or low food security, according to the report.</p><p>Among the city’s racial groups, Black residents reported the highest level of food insecurity at 61%, according to the depository’s report. In contrast, only 14% of white households reported having limited access to food.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ab0000" name="image-ab0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/36f90c4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e225c6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8ec83ea/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe2%2F6c%2Fdc3ac1c84b2db65c9d4bcdefad08%2Fhungerreport-260914-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Volunteers help pack food in an assembly line-fashion at the Greater Chicago Food Depository’s warehouse in Archer Heights, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. The organization delivers a free 10-pound box of fresh vegetables and fruits across the city but primarily to residents living in Englewood, Austin, Garfield Park and Roseland. They currently have more than 5,000 households on their waitlist.</p><p>Food insecurity is tied to a lack of other resources, Dawson said, nothing residents are also grappling with high levels of unemployment while also seeing a reduction in social services and medical care. That’s why to address food insecurity, officials have to also look at job creation, Dawson said.</p><p>“We don’t necessarily just have a money problem; we have an allocation problem when it comes to some of the resources in philanthropy and in social services as a whole,” Dawson said.</p><p>The survey also found about 47% of households with a child reported dealing with food insecurity. Maehr said they will urge lawmakers to make policy changes to address food insecurity for children or risk losing a generation.</p><p>“The data is so clear on what will happen to children if they do not have adequate access to quality, nutritious food in the first five to 10 years of their life,” she said. “It is not a 2026 problem — it is a 2036 problem, it is a 2046 problem, it is a 2056 problem.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3f0000" name="image-3f0000"></a> <picture of the new type of economy people are living in: one in which workers aren’t making enough to keep their refrigerators and pantries stocked.</p><p>About 31% of those who were food insecure were employed in some capacity, and about 27% of food insecure residents were retired, the report found. The depository’s findings also indicated those who face food insecurity are delaying or skipping payments for utilities and medical care. About 29% of those who are food insecure are also delaying or skipping rent or mortgage payments.</p><p>“They are having to turn to this system, the emergency food system, and other trade-off decisions, including, in some instances, families who make the choice, parents who make the choice not to feed themselves so that their children can have food,” Maehr said. “They’re making these choices every day in order to be able to get by in America.”</p><p>Dawson, from Dion’s Chicago Dream, said the report in many ways confirms what he and others working in the emergency food system see every day.</p><p>“Now it’s on us to make sure that we respond in a way that can honor all of these residents who are currently seeing themselves food insecure,” Dawson said.</p>

entries.title: How three millennials opened Little Village art space Te-Qu

obstacles. Just steps from the Little Village Arch at 3100 W. 26th St., Te-Qu sits in the formerly vacant building at 3126 W. 26th St. It has been, historically, a botanica, a COVID-19 testing site, a barbershop and at some point in the 1950s, a gas station. So it made sense to start a business there.</p><p>But the Little Village Chamber of Commerce informed Te-Qu that it sits in a residential zone, grinding to a halt the process of securing a business license. According to data from the Cook County Assessor’s Office, however, the address is being assessed as a commercial property and straddles the line between residential and mixed-use (commercial and residential) zones.</p><p>Because they couldn't host commercial exhibitions inside or officially launch as a store yet, Silva and his partners decided to “do what our people have been doing since forever here on 26th Street,” Anaya said. “We had to do the old Little Village method.”</p><p>That tried-and-true method, utilized by street artists and vendors for decades, means meeting the neighborhood where it already exists by taking their art to the streets. Anaya bought some clothing racks from Wal-Mart to display T-shirts and art, and the next day they attracted dozens of residents from across Chicago. They ordered pizza for guests, and representatives from The Foundation of Little Village and State Rep. Edgar González dropped by to express their support.</p><p>“We had to go back to the drawing board,” Anaya said. “That's actually where it clicked for a moment where it's like: ‘Okay, well, we don't have the piece of paper, but we have our community here.’”</p><p>But when city officials kept questioning why they couldn’t simply find a different storefront, Daniel and the team stood their ground. Now, Silva and his partners are working with the city to get the property rezoned, a process that involves Ald. Michael D. Rodriguez (22nd), Mayor Brandon Johnson and the city's rezoning committee.</p><p>The project is funded by grants from the Department of Business Affairs and Consumer Protection, and a storefront grant from the Little Village Chamber of Commerce.</p><p>Art was still happening as they waited. Mr. Pintamuro and other local artists have painted murals on the walls inside and outside of the building. "The license is good and all, but I think ultimately building and bridging that connection that brings people here is just as important, if not more,” Anaya said.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: What to know about the Chicago White Sox stadium proposal
entries.summary: <p>White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia’s</u></a> company, Canal Edge LLC, has proposed a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>the Railyards as the site for a new White Sox stadium</u></a>, which would be built where an Amtrak railyard now operates.</p><p>The rail company is simultaneously shifting its maintenance operations from the relatively isolated site of the proposed stadium to a 24/7 facility that would stretch into residential areas in Chinatown through Bridgeport.</p><p>In recent months, a coalition has formed to address the environmental and economic impact a Sox stadium move and expanded Amtrak presence would have on Bridgeport and Chinatown.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><p></p><h3>Why do the White Sox want a new stadium?</h3><p>The team is under lease at the state-owned Rate Field only through 2029, with the option to extend through 2030 before a new lease is signed.</p><h3>Where would the new stadium be located?</h3><p>The stadium would be situated within a parcel of land alongside the Chicago River, stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered by the Chicago River on its east side and Canal Street to its west.</p><h3>Who is behind the proposal?</h3><p>Justin Ishbia. He’s a minority owner of the White Sox and co-founder of Shore Capital Partners, the Loop-based private equity firm that has boosted his net worth beyond $4 billion. Shore Capital is behind the Railyards project and is helping to finance Amtrak’s new maintenance facility in Bridgeport. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>repeatedly stated interest</u></a> in a new stadium for the Sox.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3d0000" name="image-3d0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Justin Ishbia and his wife Kristen Ishbia sit courtside in 2025 during a Chicago Bulls home game.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Who is paying for the stadium?</h3><p>Ishbia's company has the land under contract. The property is across the Chicago River from where the Chicago Fire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" target="_blank" ><u>broke ground</u></a> earlier this year on its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/17/mayor-brandon-johnson-425m-tif-subsidy-the-78" target="_blank" ><u>$750 million stadium</u></a> at The 78.</p><p>The ballpark itself would be privately financed, a source with direct knowledge of the planning told the Chicago Sun-Times. But there would be an ask for public funding for local infrastructure, including for nearby roads, bridges and potentially a new Metra station, though details haven’t been finalized.</p><h3>What do the White Sox say about all this?</h3><p>The team, which previously said it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>solely focused</u></a> on the concept of a stadium alongside the Chicago Fire’s stadium at The 78, said last weekend it will evaluate the outcomes of the Railyards site’s environmental and transit studies to decide whether to consider it as a viable option for their next home.</p><p>The White Sox are owned by Jerry Reinsdorf, who remains in control of the team's stadium decisions until he decides to sell the team. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-ownership-transfer-new-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>the option</u></a> to sell to Ishbia as soon as 2029.</p><h3>What else is planned beyond a stadium?</h3><p>The mixed-use proposal also would include a Northwestern Medicine “healthcare presence” as well as transit-oriented residential, commercial and retail development. But the concept is in its early stages. A monthslong study on the feasibility of transportation and environmental evaluations is just beginning, the company said in a statement.</p><h3>How is Amtrak involved?</h3><p>As Ishbia looks to take over Amtrak land in the South Loop, his rail company has secured land in Bridgeport and is now looking to start work on building a 24/7 maintenance facility there as soon as this fall with the financing help of one of Ishbia's companies. Operations could start as soon as 2027, Amtrak previously said.</p><p>Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.doi.gov/oepc/nepa/categorical-exclusions" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allows it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>While the company said it will still conduct “<a class="Link" href="https://mwmaintenancefacility.com/" target="_blank" ><u>standard due-diligence investigations</u></a>,” residents worry the new facility could tank property values, particularly because of the potential for Rate Field being shuttered and the sound, smells or health hazards emanating from the train maintenance facility.</p><p></p><h3>What do elected officials have to say?</h3><p>Eleventh Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, whose ward encompasses Bridgeport and Rate Field, said the Sox's move out and Amtrak’s move in would be “devastating” for the area and called it a “betrayal.”</p><p>Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), whose ward would encompass the new stadium site, said he would have an open mind but would focus on “what’s in the best interests” of his ward and the city. </p><div entries.summary: <p>The fourth annual <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoexhibitionweek.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Exhibition Week</u></a> kicks off Monday with more than 50 participating galleries opening their doors for art through the weekend. Last year’s Chicago Exhibition Week attracted 10,000 attendees over three days.</p><p>Produced by Gertie, a contemporary art platform started by Abby Pucker, the week’s highlight is a series of opening receptions on Wednesday and Thursday, when major blue-chip, mid-sized and many non-traditional spaces invite the public in to see exhibitions by the likes of Jaume Plensa, Clotilde Jiménez and A new exhibition space called Te-Qu is creating space for artists with non-traditional entryways into the art world in Little Village, while the Latinx Festival of the Arts, produced by Zhou B. Art Center during Hispanic Heritage Month, runs through Nov. 15. Even the School of the Art Institute of Chicago is hosting a fall exhibition celebration on Wednesday.</p><p>Pucker said the expanded Exhibition Week is a good opportunity for Chicagoans and those intimidated by the art world to sample the scene, even if they have never visited a gallery. “Being curious is so underrated,” Pucker said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-360000" name="module-360000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoexhibitionweek.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Chicago Exhibition Week</u></b></a></h3><b>When:</b> Through Sept. 20<br><b>Where:</b> Select Chicago galleries<br><b>Tickets:</b> Galleries are free to enter, but some events are ticketed</div> </div><p>If you’re out of town or too busy to experience this year’s Chicago Exhibition Week, fear not: Many participating galleries are keeping the exhibitions that open this week through the fall. Some shows will be open well into the new year.</p><h3><b>Here are 10 gallery shows and events not to miss this fall:</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Peoria St.<br><b>When: </b>Through Dec. 13</p><p>Combining comedy with contemporary art, this 12-week exhibition features rotating experiences, performances and screenings. “82 Nights Only” is an attempt to disrupt the fixed exhibition format and change the stigma of a stuffy art show, said Gertie’s head of programming, partnerships and membership, Chanelle Lacy.</p><p>Featured artists include <a class="Link" href="https://www.nyeemamorgan.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Nyeema Morgan</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.contemporaryartlibrary.org/artist/ken-kagami-3636" target="_blank" ><u>Ken Kagami</u></a>, Chicago favorite <a class="Link" href="https://www.moma.org/collection/artists/37145" target="_blank" ><u>Pope.L</u></a>, and many more.</p><p>You’ll get a totally different experience every night of the exhibition, Pucker and Lacy said. It’s a show “about comedy and art” that includes over 20 artists.</p><p>The opening night reception on Wednesday will feature New York-based artist and ventriloquist Sophie Becker. Paulina St.<br><b>When: </b>Through Oct. 31</p><p>Born in Honolulu, Hawaii, and raised in Philadelphia, <a class="Link" href="https://www.clotildejimenez.art/" target="_blank" ><u>Clotilde Jiménez</u></a> describes his worldview as “bifocal,” and that’s evident in all of his work.“Éramos silencios” draws on a family secret. The man he’d known his entire life as his Tío Juan was revealed to be his biological grandfather. The two deepened their relationship even more after the revelation. That paternal relationship, improved over many visits and months-long stays to the island, allowed Jiménez to develop a “racial vocabulary” that flips the American experience entirely on its head.</p><p>Look out for pieces such as “Los Varones,” which depict his Tío Juan, grandfather Gabriel and grandmother Renée Jiménez, and “Invitación al Altar,” inspired in part by Mexico City modernist mural art, where the artist now lives and works.</p><p>Oranges grow all over Puerto Rico, but the ones in Mayagüez are particularly important to Jiménez. The fruits appear across many of the works in “Éramos silencios,” especially in self-portraits.</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Paulina St. <br><b>When: </b>Through Oct. 24</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/dance/2026/05/04/driehaus-museum-brendan-fernandes-performances-in-the-round" target="_blank" ><u>Brendan Fernandes</u></a> is not easily categorized: He blends visual art with dance, design, textiles and music to create multi-sensory experiences, blending his own curiosity with experimentation.</p><p>“As a young kid, I was always dancing and drawing and painting,” he told WBEZ in May.</p><p>Fernandes’ work will be featured at several events this fall. Meloche’s midsized West Town gallery will showcase “The Noise Will Sound,” the Kenyan-Canadian artist’s latest series of film photographs. Figures are draped in checkered Shuka cloth, worn by the Maasai people of Kenya. The featured textiles were commissioned by the Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia in 2025 and, for “The Noise Will Sound,” were performed as a duet, with dancers hiding and revealing each other through movement.</p><p>The artist will also debut a series of paintings on Belgian linen. Hernandez</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://carlossalazarlermont.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Carlos Salazar-Lermont</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.haiwenlin.com/about" target="_blank" ><u>Hai-Wen Lin</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.jasjyotjasjyot.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Jasjyot Singh Hans</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://lolaogbara.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Lola Ayisha Ogbara</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.monikaplioplyte.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Monika Plioplyte</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://marianneboeskygallery.com/artists/61-jay-heikes/biography/" target="_blank" ><u>Jay Heikes</u></a>.</p><p>A curated collection of sounds, movement and visual art, the show is also an official part of Gertie’s Chicago Exhibition Week. Ellis Ave.<br><b>When: </b>Through Nov. 1</p><p>If you haven’t visited The Ren yet, this is the season to go to<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2026/09/09/renaissance-society-chicago-gallery-myriam-ben-salah" target="_blank" ><u> the adventurous exhibition space</u></a> on the University of Chicago campus. Karimah Ashadu’s solo exhibition at The Ren mixes film with installation. Her moving images are rooted in a West African and European experience. Ashadu grew up between Nigeria and the United Kingdom, and today resides and works between Lagos, Nigeria and Hamburg, Germany.</p><p>A major piece of Ashadu’s show at The Ren includes the U.S. debut of “MUSCLE,” an approximately 22-minute documentary-style film that tells the story of bodybuilders training in Lagos’ slums. The film is accompanied by several new works that draw on the places and people presented in “MUSCLE.” For many of the bodybuilders, the sport is less about looks and more about labor and self-investment.</p><p>Ashadu’s work at The Ren is being presented in tandem with Ashadu’s “Machine Boys” at the Art Institute of Chicago.</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div And he’s embraced AI-generated images as he grapples with capitalism and advancements in technology in his work.</p><p>Born in Hong Kong and raised in London, Cheung’s practice is rooted in a concept he calls the “technosublime,” which lives at the intersection of globalization and the natural world. Born and raised near the border region around El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, the artist's pop art style is inspired by his everyday life in the Pilsen neighborhood and the South Side of Chicago.</p><p>Classic cars, public housing, tires and other objects are constants throughout Villa’s work, crowning subjects in portraits such as “The Poet.” Keep your eyes peeled for other concept portraits such as “The Butterfly Catcher” and “The Visionary,” which draw on the artist’s experiences in a border town and are meant to be read as poems with multitudes.</p><p>Many of Villa’s works have been shown at the National Museum of Mexican Art in Pilsen, where he once directed the museum’s youth arts program, Yollicalli Arts Reach.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ac0000" name="module-ac0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Your guide to fall culture in Chicago </b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f6c56c02-ac5f-11f1-988e-bd5e5ce8e98f"><li>The next big thing is happening on Chicago’s small stages. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/09/04/theater-to-see-chicago-fall-storefront-tickets-new-plays-musicals" target="_blank" ><u>Here are 10 plays and musicals</u></a> not to miss this theater season.</li><li>The ultimate guide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2026/09/10/chicago-fall-film-festivals-events-things-to-do-movies-ciff-cuff-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s fall film festivals</u></a>, from Oscar contenders to local standouts</li><li>Evanston’s $32 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>new Northlight Theatre</u></a> wasn’t built for big crowds. It’s built for new plays.</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>“Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism”</u></a> is the Art Institute’s first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years and explores some of her historical Chicago ties.</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ben Johnson (59 points) 'didn't get into this profession trying to be mediocre'
entries.summary: <p>CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Minutes after scoring 59 points, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson wasn’t shy about his goals for his team.</p><p>“We didn't get into this profession trying to be mediocre, average,” he said after Sunday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/13/bears-panthers-podcast-offense-ben-johnson-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >59-37 win against the Panthers</a>. “That's every NFL team. That is what it is. We make decisions over the course of a week, what's best for our football team to win the game. That's the most important thing, and that goes into everything that we do.”</p><p>The Bears’ 59 points were the third-most in the history of the franchise and the most in 46 years. It was the most Johnson had scored as a play-caller; the 2024 Lions scored 52 twice, once against the Titans and again against the Jaguars.</p><p>The 2022 Bears, by contrast, totaled 52 points over their first three games of the season. The 2023 team had 47. The 2024 team had 53. </p><p>Johnson was asked whether his attitude prompted him to go for it on fourth-and-one from his own 21 in the second quarter. He said it was not, but reiterated what he said during training camp — that the he has high, almost-impossible goals for his team. He wants to surpass the 2013 Broncos, who averaged a league-record 37.9 points per game. He wants to go undefeated. And he wants to win multiple championships.</p><p>Most other coaches in the league want to as well. What makes Johnson different, if anything, is that he says it out loud.</p><p>“We want to be the highest scoring, we want to have the most wins, we want to win Super Bowls,” he said. “We want to. Like, that's what we do.”<br></p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams for MVP? It's early, but it's possible
entries.summary: <p>On Sunday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> did the near-impossible.</p><p>He quarterbacked a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> franchise once synonymous with offensive ineptitude to 59 points in their season opening win against the Panthers. He became the first quarterback in the 106-year history of his team to both post a passer rating above 124 and rush for 65 yards. And he completed 72 percent of his passes, clearing coach Ben Johnson’s lofty standard of 70.</p><p>Along the way, he accomplished one of the most difficult things in sports — he lived up to the hype.</p><p>From the moment Williams lofted his answered prayer to Cole Kmet — in a playoff game the Bears lost to the Rams — the quarterback has been pegged by many for sudden stardom. EA Sports put him on their “Madden” cover. Hallmark put him in their Bears movie. He became so ubiquitous that at least one coach, the Jaguars’ Liam Coen, complained.</p><p>Despite Williams never even been elected to a Pro Bowl, he became a trendy offseason pick to win MVP — and, fair or not, was bound to be judged by that standard Week 1. Sunday, amazingly, he didn’t nothing to dispel the notion he could win it. In fact, it’s hard to imagine a time in modern NFL history when a Bears quarterback has seemed more likely to contend for the MVP.</p><p>Fans waking up morning found Williams with the fourth-best odds to win the MVP, behind only the Bills’ Josh Allen, the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson and the Bengals’ Joe Burrow. Even with two quarterbacks in the league yet to play at that point — the Chiefs’ Patrick Mahomes and the Broncos’ Bo Nix were slated for a Monday night clash — that’s a staggering place for Williams to land. He has 9:1 odds to win it.</p><p>It’s early — perhaps way-too-early — for Bears fans to dream of their first NFL MVP since Walter Payton in 1977. But it’s at least possible.</p><p>First impressions matter. Here’s how the favorites for MVP fared in Week 1:</p><p>• Allen had the best win of any quarterback all weekend, leading the Bills to a road victory against a Texans defense that was the best in the AFC last year. He did it in dramatic fashion, too, taking possession at his own 4 with 3:14 left and the Bills trailing by one. it took him just seven plays to march 96 yards, throwing a 34-yard touchdown to Joshua Palmer that proved to be the game-winner. The former MVP winner finished with a 130.5 passer rating, the third-best among all quarterbacks entering Monday night’s game.</p><p>• Jackson threw for 324 yards and ran for 40 more, scoring one touchdown each through the air and on the ground, in his Week 1 win at Indianapolis. In their first game under play-caller Declan Doyle, who served as Johnson’s coordinator last season, the Colts scored 41 points. Among all teams that played through Sunday, only Johnson’s Bears scored more. Jackson has won two MVPs in his career.</p><p>• The Bengals were perhaps the trendiest pick to flip their record from last season after going 6-11 and posting a historically terrible defense. Burrow’s stats weren’t remarkable in a 33-27 win against the Buccaneers — he threw for 254 yards and a 89.5 passer rating — but a season-long team turnaround would give him an edge that Allen, Jackson and Williams couldn’t match.</p><p>The Jaguars’ Trevor Lawrence, who had a ridiculous 150.6 passer rating and four passing touchdowns against the God-awful Browns, and the 49ers’ Brock Purdy, who threw for a 105.6 passer rating and three touchdowns in the Down Under upset of the Rams, are also contenders on our way-too-early watchlist. Defending MVP Matthew Stafford, as terrible as he was in Melbourne, can’t be ruled out, either. The Chargers’ Justin Herbert, the Patriots’ Drake Maye and the Cowboys’ Dak Prescott were all stunned in their opener.</p><p>Then there’s Williams, who grabbed the attention of the NFL on Sunday with both his arm and his legs. He reached 20.8 mph on his 29-yard touchdown run, the fourth-fastest speed of any player in Week 1 through Sunday.</p><p>On CBS Sports, analyst Bryant McFadden compared him to Stephen Curry, saying, like the Warriors star, he can score from anywhere. In his first game as an NBC analyst Sunday night, former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin praised his physical talent and pointed to his increased comfort in Johnson's system.</p><p>“Chicago fans should be excited,” Tomlin said. “The rest of the NFC North should be very frightened by what we saw.”</p><p>On Sunday, Williams became the fourth NFL quarterback ever to top 250 passing yards and 50 rushing yards; throw for two touchdowns and run for two more; and post a passer rating of at least 120 in the same game. The other three were Allen in 2024, the Panthers’ Cam Newton in 2012 and the Eagles’ Michael Vick in 2010. </p><p>Two of the three were MVPs. Williams might one day join them. It’s early. But given how long the Bears have been starving for a quarterback, the mere possibility is remarkable in itself. </p>

entries.title: Man grabbed woman, sexually abused her on CTA Blue Line in Wicker Park
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police were warning of sexual abuse on the CTA Blue Line that occurred earlier this month in the Wicker Park neighborhood. </p><p>A man entered the Cumberland station and rode to the Division station where he "waited for his target, a woman in a skirt," Chicago police said in a statement. </p><p>The man then ran toward her as she began walking up the stairs and grabbed her but she was somehow able to escape his grasp and he ran away, police said. </p><p>The incident occurred around 6:10 p.m. Sept. 5 at the Division station, 1200 N. Milwaukee Ave.</p><p>The man is said to be between 5-foot-5 and 5-foot-8, 210 pounds, has long black hair and two upper arm tattoos, police said. He was last seen wearing an Adidas cap. </p><p>Anyone with information is asked to call Mass Transit Detectives at 312-745-4447.<br></p>

entries.title: Former Providence football coach Tyler Plantz speaks out on his firing
entries.summary: <p>Providence announced the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/13/providence-fires-football-coach-tyler-plantz" >firing of football coach Tyler Plantz</a> on Sunday afternoon. It was a stunning move. The Celtics are undefeated, ranked No. 5 in the Super 25 and fresh off an appearance in the Class 5A state title game. </p><p>Providence AD Doug Terkin didn't provide a solid reason for Plantz's dismissal, only saying the football program was moving in a new direction. </p><p>Plantz has not responded to multiple requests for a comment from the Sun-Times. <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/Matt_Fortuna/status/2099535946307752162" target="_blank" >He released a statement on Monday to journalist Matt Fortuna. </a></p><p>Plantz says that Providence president Fr. John Merkelis asked him to resign on Saturday. </p><p>"During our meeting for less than an hour, Father Merkelis informed me that other staff members had told him about a few disgruntled colleagues and a few football player's parents," Plantz said in the statement. "He cited problems with disorganization related to scheduling games for lower level teams, which was not my responsibility. He also said he was not satisfied with how I managed college recruiting this year and structured lower level practices."</p><p>Plantz says those were the only concerns indicated by Merkelis and that as of Monday morning he has not received any notice from Providence that he has been terminated. </p><p>"I am confounded by this decision and how it has been handled," Plantz said in the statement. "I remain proud of my contributions to Providence Catholic Celtic's success since I was named head coach."</p><p>It is extremely rare for a high school to fire a head varsity football coach during the season. </p><p>Plantz, a former Notre Dame football player and Providence graduate, was 35-19 in his time as head coach. He graduated from Providence in 2010 and from Notre Dame in 2014. He began his career in South Bend as a walk-on but moved up to special teams and earned a scholarship for his senior year. Plantz was on Brian Kelly’s coaching staff at Notre Dame before taking the job at Providence in 2022.</p><p>Providence announced on Sunday that offensive coordinator Adam Thissen is the interim head coach for the rest of the season.</p><p>‘‘Coach Nissen is an experienced leader who knows our student-athletes, our coaching staff and our program,’’ Ternik’s statement said. ‘‘Our focus is on providing our players with stability and support as they continue through the season. We are confident in Coach Nissen’s ability to step into this role and lead our football program during this transition.’’</p><p>Nissen was recently a successful head coach at St. Laurence. He led the Vikings to the Class 4A title game in 2023 and was 35-28 in six seasons.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Statement from Tyler Plantz, who was fired as head coach by Providence Catholic HS on Sunday.<br><br>The former Notre Dame fullback says he was asked to resign, refused, and still has not received notice of his firing from PC, his alma mater: <a href="https://t.co/Lihl7uq2Uy">pic.twitter.com/Lihl7uq2Uy</a></p>— Matt Fortuna (@Matt_Fortuna) <a href="https://x.com/Matt_Fortuna/status/2099535946307752162?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.summary: <p>White Sox minority owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Justin Ishbia’s</u></a> company, Canal Edge LLC, has proposed a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" target="_blank" ><u>the Railyards as the site for a new White Sox stadium</u></a>, which would be built where an Amtrak railyard now operates.</p><p>Amtrak is simultaneously shifting its maintenance operations from the relatively isolated site of the proposed stadium to a 24/7 facility that would have the same footprint as their current railyard, but in Bridgeport/Chinatown. </p><p>In recent months, a coalition has formed to address the environmental and economic impact a Sox stadium move and expanded Amtrak presence would have on Bridgeport and Chinatown.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><h3>Why do the White Sox want a new stadium?</h3><p>The team is under lease at the state-owned Rate Field only through 2029, with the option to extend through 2030 before a new lease is signed.</p><h3>Where would the new stadium be located?</h3><p>The stadium would be situated within a parcel of land alongside the Chicago River, stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered by the Chicago River on its east side and Canal Street to its west.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-910000" </div><p></p><h3>Who is behind the proposal?</h3><p>Justin Ishbia. class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Who is paying for the stadium?</h3><p>Canal Edge has the land under contract. The property is across the Chicago River from where the Chicago Fire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/03/03/chicago-fire-football-club-breaks-ground-650-million-stadium-78" target="_blank" ><u>broke ground</u></a> earlier this year on its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/17/mayor-brandon-johnson-425m-tif-subsidy-the-78" target="_blank" ><u>$750 million stadium</u></a> at The 78.</p><p>The ballpark itself would be privately financed, a source with direct knowledge of the planning told the Chicago Sun-Times. But there would be an ask for public funding for local infrastructure, including for nearby roads, bridges and potentially a new Metra station, though details haven’t been finalized.</p><h3>What do the White Sox say about all this?</h3><p>The team, which previously said it was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>solely focused</u></a> on the concept of a stadium alongside the Chicago Fire’s stadium at The 78, said last weekend it will evaluate the outcomes of the Railyards site’s environmental and transit studies to decide whether to consider it as a viable option for their next home.</p><p>The White Sox are owned by Jerry Reinsdorf, who remains in control of the team's stadium decisions until he decides to sell the team. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-ownership-transfer-new-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>the option</u></a> to sell to Ishbia as soon as 2029.</p><h3>What else is planned beyond a stadium?</h3><p>The mixed-use proposal also would include a Northwestern Medicine “healthcare presence” as well as transit-oriented residential, commercial and retail development. But the concept is in its early stages. A monthslong study on the feasibility of transportation and environmental evaluations is just beginning, the company said in a statement.</p><h3>How is Amtrak involved?</h3><p>As Ishbia looks to take over Amtrak land in the South Loop, Amtrak has secured land in Bridgeport and is now looking to start work on building a 24/7 maintenance facility there as soon as this fall with the financing help of one of Ishbia's companies. Operations could start as soon as 2027, Amtrak previously said.</p><p>Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.doi.gov/oepc/nepa/categorical-exclusions" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allows it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.” There was, however, an environmental review process that included a noise/vibration/air quality review.</p><p>While the company said it will still conduct “<a class="Link" href="https://mwmaintenancefacility.com/" target="_blank" ><u>standard due-diligence investigations</u></a>,” residents worry the new facility could tank property values, particularly because of the potential for Rate Field being shuttered and the sound, smells or health hazards emanating from the train maintenance facility.</p><p></p><h3>What do elected officials have to say?</h3><p>Eleventh Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, whose ward encompasses Bridgeport and Rate Field, said the Sox's move out and Amtrak’s move in would be “devastating” for the area and called it a “betrayal.”</p><p>Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), whose ward would encompass the new stadium site, said he would have an open mind but would focus on “what’s in the best interests” of his ward and the city. </p><div entries.title: 1 person killed in 2-car Dan Ryan crash at 55th Street
entries.summary: <p>Two vehicles collided Monday morning, leaving one person dead and at least one person injured in the Washington Park neighborhood. </p><p>Interstate 94 northbound, at 55<sup>th</sup> Street (Express), Chicago, Cook County</p><p>About 8:15 a.m. two vehicles crashed in the inbound express lanes at 55th Street, according to a statement from Illinois State Police. </p><p>One person has died while at least one additional person was injured, according to the statement. </p><p>The northbound express lanes have been shut down from 71<sup>st</sup> Street. </p><p>There was no further information available. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Three critical, including 8-year-old boy, following Portage Park blaze
entries.summary: <p>Fire investigators are trying to figure out what caused a fire Monday morning that left an 8-year-old boy, a 17-year-old boy and a man critically injured in the Portage Park neighborhood. </p><p>Crews responded to a home in the 4000 block of North Austin Avenue about 6:15 a.m. and rescued the boy, a 34-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, Chicago police said in a statement. </p><p>They were all taken in critical condition to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, with burns and smoke inhalation, according to the statement, which added that eight people were left homeless. </p><p>The cause of the fire remains under investigation by the fire department. <br></p>

entries.title: This group is building benches at bus stops that don't have one. Will the city let them?
entries.summary: <p>A pair of homemade wooden benches painted bright yellow and blue appeared last week at CTA bus stops in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/ukrainian-village" >Ukrainian Village</a>.</p><p>The benches were built and installed by a neighborhood group tired of seeing bus stops without them. </p><p>Several people posting online praised the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance for building the benches.</p><p>The group wants to build more, but is waiting to see what the city does.</p><p>Technically, the benches are illegal.</p><p>They were placed without seeking permission from the city, said Sam Kovnar, 25, founder of the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance.</p><p>"A lot of public transit agencies fall short on quality-of-life issues," Kovnar said. "If there's no bench at the bus stop, that makes a difference whenever an older person chooses to use the stop. It makes the 5-, 10- or 15-minute wait possible or not."</p><p>One bench is at Damen Avenue and Thomas Street, the other at Division Street and Oakley Boulevard.</p><p>People roundly praised the benches in <a class="Link" href="https://www.reddit.com/r/chicago/comments/1wb3317/we_built_some_bus_stop_benches_this_week_what/" target="_blank" >posts</a> on <a class="Link" href="https://www.reddit.com/r/chicago/comments/1waqquy/a_huge_thank_you_to_whoever_placed_this_bench_at/" target="_blank" >Reddit</a>.</p><p>One commenter said, "As a person who needs to be able to sit while waiting I thank you for the work you are doing."</p><p>Kovnar, reflecting on the positive feedback, said, "It was also distressing to read how much difference a bench could make."</p><div The CTA and city Transportation Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the benches.</p><p>"We're waiting to see what happens," said Kovnar, who works in software. "Obviously if the city sends us an angry letter, we will stop. ... But I think it's hard to argue that the benches are not wanted."</p><p>Kovnar said he was inspired to build the benches from his time living in Milwaukee, where he helped other advocates build and place homemade benches at bus stops.</p><p>Eddie Lehwald, a member of the Northwest Neighborhood Alliance, said he built one of the two benches a couple of years ago but hesitated to place it at a bus Northwest Neighborhood Alliance, to inspire Lehwald to finally place it in public.</p><p>"I was glad to make this bench useful," he said.</p><p>It's a matter of dignity to have a place to sit while waiting for the bus, Lehwald said.</p><p>"Anyone who's waited for a bus has experienced the inconvenience of not having a place to sit down," Lehwald said. "If you're a parent and have little kids, or you have a body that's not functioning at 100%, a place to sit is a basic amenity for human dignity."</p><p>So what's next?</p><p>"What I'd love is for the city to say, 'A-ha! We do need to do this and we hear you. This isn't hurting anybody. It's helping people. We tacitly agree not to remove these,'" Lehwald said.</p><p>The city could even go a step further and bolt down the benches, he said.</p><p>"The worst thing the city could do is remove them. I think they would be missing an opportunity to positively engage their communities," he said.</p>

entries.title: President Trump endorses Darren Bailey in Illinois governor race — ‘Pritzker’s a disaster’
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump says he’s “all for Bailey” once again in the Illinois governor race, handing Republican firebrand Darren Bailey an endorsement that’s unlikely to do the former downstate legislator many favors as he tries to court Chicago-area moderates in his rematch against incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p>Speaking to reporters Sunday before returning from a trip to Ireland, Trump said of his longtime supporter: “I’ve already endorsed him. I’m all for Bailey.”</p><p>Bailey <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2022/6/25/23183316/darren-bailey-trump-endorsement-igop-governor-primary-election" target="_blank" ><u>rallied alongside Trump in 2022</u></a> before losing to Pritzker by nearly 13 percentage points, and Bailey credited Trump with inspiring him to stay in the 2026 race in the face of immense tragedy last fall after Bailey’s son, daughter-in-law and two grandchildren died in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/11/darren-bailey-gop-primary-governor-race-illinois-helicopter-tragedy" target="_blank" ><u>a helicopter crash</u></a>.</p><p>“Bailey is a very good candidate,” Trump said. “He had a horrible tragedy. It’s amazing that he can go forward. A large portion of his family was wiped out.”</p><p>But Bailey has largely distanced himself from the president while focusing on crime, education and economic issues in his latest gubernatorial campaign.</p><p>The GOP nominee’s team scarcely publicized his trip last week to Dallas for the Republican Midterm Convention, where he sat in the president’s box near downstate U.S. Rep. Mike Bost — who carried Trump’s endorsement while staving off a 2024 congressional <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2024/03/19/illinois-chicago-primary-2024-bost-bailey-trump-foster-casten" target="_blank" ><u>primary challenge from Bailey</u></a>.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Hello from the President’s Box at the Midterm Convention! Thank you for the invitation, President Trump! <a href="https://t.co/DrHj4nBqpO">pic.twitter.com/DrHj4nBqpO</a></p>— Mike Bost (@BostForCongress) <a href="https://x.com/BostForCongress/status/2098202594078249344?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 11, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Meanwhile, Bailey has gone out of his way to publicize his differences in opinion with Trump.</p><p>In April, Bailey said the president “was wrong” to criticize <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/04/12/trump-lambasts-pope-leo-xiv-extending-feud-over-iran-war-with-first-american-pontiff" target="_blank" ><u>Pope Leo XIV</u></a> and urged him to apologize to the Chicago-born pontiff. And last month, Bailey said he doesn’t “see eye to eye” with Trump’s support of data center expansion.</p><p>It’s a logical campaign strategy for the downstate farmer who is trying to make inroads with suburban voters who rejected him by 20 percentage points or more last time around, in areas that long served as the Illinois GOP base before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/20/bob-grogan-illinois-republican-party-new-chairperson-dupage-county-auditor" target="_blank" ><u>defecting from Trump</u></a>.</p><p>That leaves a tight rope to walk for Bailey and his downstate, rural base that remains staunchly in Trump’s corner.</p><p>"I appreciate President Trump's endorsement of my campaign for governor, but that's not what this race is about; it's about the endless ways JB Pritzker has failed Illinois families over the last eight years,” Bailey said in a statement.</p><p>“From endless tax hikes to the highest property taxes in the nation, preferential treatment for career criminals while our officers are underpaid and under appreciated, all while businesses shutter their doors and everyone from workers to the Chicago Bears vote with their feet, our state is worse off today under JB Pritzker's leadership. Change will only happen when Illinois voters step into the voting booth and vote for it,” he said.</p><p>Pritzker’s campaign has sought to remind voters of Bailey’s ties to Trump <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/19/chris-welch-state-fair-illinois-house-sexual-harassment-harry-benton" >at every turn</a>.</p><p>“Just a few days after Darren Bailey returned home from Trumpapalooza, Donald Trump endorsed Bailey and sang his praises,” Pritzker campaign spokesperson Leah Hurwitz said in a statement. “This won’t come as a surprise to Illinoisans who know all about Bailey’s intense admiration for Trump. Despite the damage the president has done to our state, Bailey still supports Trump’s tariffs, cheered on his invasion of federal agents in our streets, and vowed to ‘roll the red carpet out’ for him.”</p><p>Pritzker’s team raised the question of whether Trump will campaign with Bailey next week, when Trump is scheduled to return to the Chicago area for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/30/trump-chairman-western-suburbs-presidents-cup-golf-tournament-sports" target="_blank" ><u>the first time in his second term</u></a> to chair the Presidents Cup golf tournament at Medinah Country Club, running Sept. 22-27.</p><p>Pritzker, who is considering a 2028 run for president, has raised his national profile as a vociferous Trump opponent.</p><p>“I think JB Pritzker’s a disaster as a governor,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3QnJGu0Q09o&t=39s" target="_blank" >Trump said</a>. “You look at what’s happening with crime — JB Pritzker should lose. For some reason, Democrats win there, I don’t know why.”</p>

entries.title: Keke Palmer drew hundreds to an ‘empowering’ Pilates class in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A mat Pilates class taught by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/celebrities/2025/02/05/keke-palmer-chicago-one-of-them-days-creme-of-nature-eddie-murphy-pickup" target="_blank" ><u>Keke Palmer</u></a> is just what you’d imagine: a casual, friendly environment; instruction delivered in a conversational tone; and lots of laughter.</p><p>Nearly 250 fans experienced it firsthand Sunday at the Salt Shed during the second annual exercise festival “Move at the Shed.”</p><p>The room was bathed in tranquil green lighting, which the 33-year-old actress, singer and host complimented from the stage. Wearing hot pink leggings and a matching top, she shared anecdotes and cracked jokes as she led the attendees through leg stretches, hip rolls and squats. She occasionally sang along to the background music — a playlist of songs from her albums.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Palmer, who got her start working with Chicago talent agencies, isn’t the only millennial celebrity cultivating a fitness brand. Rapper Gunna has built a following with his global <a class="Link" href="https://www.wunnarunclub.com/?utm_source=ig&utm_medium=social&utm_content=link_in_bio&fbclid=PAcGRvZgJleHRuA2FlbQIxMQBzcnRjBmFwcF9pZA85MzY2MTk3NDMzOTI0NTkAAac43NgVOW1EtXFOmE5-rBGFecKjq_oeoRoiiYF3Cfc9TR656bLfM744mM8Mrw_aem_b4kOJk46CE62_dG4kY5FJA" target="_blank" ><u>Wunna Run Club</u></a>, emcee ASAP Ferg is <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DdKM5HsPlfR/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>teaching cycling</u></a> and boot camp classes, and actress and singer Hilary Duff is the face of a <a class="Link" href="https://www.joinladder.com/hilary" target="_blank" ><u>“stronger, not smaller” campaign</u></a> for the Ladder workout app.</p><p>In a cultural moment defined by the promotion of GLP-1’s for weight loss, Palmer’s brand is about building community and promoting mental and physical well-being<b> </b>rather than being thin.</p><p>“Everybody's body is beautiful,” Palmer said during a fireside chat with ABC7 anchor Val Warner after her class. “Pilates is really just about being able to be mobile.
