entries.title: Week 4 takeaways: CSL South on the rise, Israel Abrams sparkles for Montini, Fox Valley shakeup
entries.summary: <p>Maine South has dominated the Central Suburban League football scene for decades, so much so that it may have hurt the Hawks.</p><p>Typically, Maine South opens as a highly ranked team, plays a few tough nonconference games, and then spends the rest of the regular season winning blowouts.</p><p>That may not be the case this season. The Hawks received a tough challenge from New Trier and Purdue-bound quarterback Jackie Ryder last Thursday. Indiana-bound quarterback Jameson Purcell was excellent and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/10/maine-south-football-new-trier" >Maine South pulled out a 35-28 victory</a>.</p><p>Keep an eye on what the rest of the CSL South does against the Hawks. Evanston is 3-1 with a nice win against Palatine, and Glenbrook South, which beat Evanston 33-9 in Week 4, has been on the rise for a few years. The Titans are 2-2, but opened the season with competitive losses to York and Fremd.</p><p>“Definitely, the conference is more competitive than when I got here,” Purcell said. “The teams are stepping up. New Trier has been off and on. This is our 11th year winning against them and every year they come out and get better.</p><p>“Evanston is showing stuff. I’m just happy about it. It is cool to see other teams succeeding. Sometimes the CSL doesn’t get much respect.”</p><h3>Israel Abrams sparkles again</h3><p>Maybe it is because the Sun-Times hasn’t covered enough of his games, but it feels as if Montini quarterback Israel Abrams isn’t receiving the attention he deserves locally.</p><p>The Miami recruit is one of the most thrilling players in the country. Abrams made two jaw-dropping plays in the Class 4A state championship game last year.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-850000" name="image-850000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/57b6d32/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6388x3585+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2Fe3%2F6df7db2e4443871741f44491df3f%2Fob-cst-081226-015.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/96cf03f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6388x3585+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2Fe3%2F6df7db2e4443871741f44491df3f%2Fob-cst-081226-015.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c37666e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6388x3585+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8d%2Fe3%2F6df7db2e4443871741f44491df3f%2Fob-cst-081226-015.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Montini’s Israell Abrams (7) works a drill during preseason football practice. And Montini needed every yard to squeak out a 47-42 win against Nazareth.</p><p>Abrams was 25 of 35 passing for 411 yards. He threw four touchdown passes and ran for three touchdowns.</p><h3>Streak breakers</h3><p>There were two historically notable results in Week 4.</p><p>Hersey, led by Kentucky recruit Jake Nawrot, beat Barrington for the first time since 1994.</p><p>Nawrot is ranked as one of the top five quarterbacks in the country. He was 25-for-32 passing for 361 yards and three touchdowns in the Huskies’ 38-7 win against Barrington.</p><p>Hersey’s nonconference schedule hasn’t turned out as tough as expected, with Carmel and the Broncos not living up to their preseason rankings. The Huskies have an excellent chance to be undefeated when they arrive at Prospect for a showdown in Week 9.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> DuPage Valley rival Neuqua Valley until Friday. The Mustangs won 34-29 on the road in thrilling fashion.</p><p>Iggy Amorrortu connected with Charlie Larson on a 29-yard touchdown pass with nine seconds left to secure the win for Metea Valley. The Mustangs scored three consecutive touchdowns in the fourth quarter to earn the comeback victory.</p><h3>New look Fox Valley</h3><p>Prairie Ridge and Cary-Grove have dominated the Fox Valley and been perennial state championship contenders over the past decade.</p><p>That stranglehold started to slip last season when Burlington Central finished second in the conference ahead of Cary-Grove, and it is totally gone now.</p><p>Cary-Grove has a young team this season and is hanging on in third place at 3-1. But Prairie Ridge is winless and in last place. The Crystal Lake school’s enrollment has been shrinking for years, and it may struggle to compete in the Fox Valley in the future.</p><p>Jacobs and Huntley are tied for first place and undefeated through the first two weeks. The Golden Eagles were expected to challenge for the Super 25 this season and are right on track. Huntley is off to an extremely intriguing start. The Red Raiders, who compete in Class 8A, have scored 218 points and allowed just six.</p>

entries.title: Review: Hip-hop play ‘How We Got On’ deftly tackles coming-of-age themes but needs a little remixing
entries.summary: <p>The year is 1988. Hip-hop is in its golden era. E.U. has the whole country doing “Da Butt,” as suggested in the group's chart-topping hit from the soundtrack of Spike Lee’s film “School Daze.” On the West Coast, N.W.A. released “Straight Outta Compton,” and Public Enemy’s “Don’t Believe the Hype” is blaring out of boomboxes on street corners coast to coast.</p><p>This is the backdrop of “How We Got On,” a play with music having its world premiere at Hyde Park’s Definition Theatre. Directed by artistic director Tyrone Phillips, the drama follows teens Hank, Julian and Luann as they’re caught in the tidal wave of hip-hop by way of the classic television show “Yo! MTV Raps.” Influenced by the show’s aesthetic of flashy jewels, fancy cars and fresh rhymes, these teens decide they will become the next rap superstars. But here’s the catch: These kids are from the suburbs. A world away from the urban areas where hip-hop is booming.</p><p>The script by veteran playwright Idris Goodwin has good bones. Hip-hop pairs well with a coming-of-age story. The genre, according to legend, was born at a house party in the Bronx in the early 1970s. In “How We Got On,” hip-hop itself was in its teenage years, just like the characters we meet. The play has a lot to say about formative years — how kids find themselves, the influence of parents, and, in the case of Black and Latino kids in predominantly white suburbs in the late ’80s, cultural isolation.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="2.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘How We Got On’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d70000" name="module-d70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Where:</b> Definition Theatre, 1160 E. 55th St.<br><b>When:</b> Through Sept. 27<br><b>Tickets:</b> From $25<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.definitiontheatre.org/" target="_blank" >definitiontheatre.org</a></div> </div><p>Goodwin has a deft hand in displaying these themes, yet as a whole the production still needs a little work, and perhaps additional actors. Selector, played by Maya Vinice Prentiss, pulls quadruple duties as narrator/DJ, and the father of all three teens. The dynamic of each dad and the different pressures they put on their children is important in this play. Having another actor would have gone a long way to draw on those relationships and provide a deeper connection. Having Selector jump in and out of those roles made the relationships feel surface level and almost like an afterthought, which takes away from the drama.</p><p>Luann, portrayed excellently by Anuoluwa T Awolola, was vastly underwritten, as was her father. She enters the action midway through the production and serves as a catalyst for Hank and Julian to complete their respective arcs. Her character is interesting and deserves a deeper journey of her own. In one scene, atop a water tower overlooking the suburb, Luann teaches Hank to freestyle by interpreting his observations. It leads to wondering what she went through to develop the skill herself. Her father (played by Prentiss) is an NBA player who hates rap. We don’t see him come around to enjoy her music or push her toward a goal. He’s just there.</p><p>Hank (Jamal Turner) and Julian (Tony Garcia) have a chemistry that carries the production. The ups and downs of their friendship and the way they push each other to be better artists (in a funny scene, we see they are terrible basketball players) are compelling. Both young actors capture the essence of Black and brown kids who are whisked out of cities for lives in the suburbs where they immediately become outsiders. They have a love for hip-hop — rapping, making beats, performing — but it's also clear they long for a connection to their own cultures that don’t exist in the place their parents have moved them to.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-270000" name="image-270000"></a> <picture This was true in his play “The Boy Who Kissed the Sky,” about a fictionalized childhood of rock icon Jimi Hendrix, and it’s apparent here as well. The dialogue of the play feels like a mixtape. Characters’ words are repeated, or looped, and at times Selector stops the action and uses the characters’ words to make beats for the audience. This device could have been used a bit more sparingly, as it halts the action of the story, but stylistically, it’s clever and a unique way to lean into the theme of the play.</p><p>The heart of the story is the teens using hip-hop for self discovery and finding a way to be seen by peers, parents and each other. It works, but still feels a little rough around the edges. The good news is this story is steeped in hip-hop. So, with a little remixing, this can become a promising production.</p>

entries.title: Death of man who died days after being shot in Uptown investigated as homicide: CPD
entries.summary: <p>The death of a man shot in Uptown earlier this month is being investigated as a homicide, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Jarrett Ceaser, 27, was found in the 4900 block of North Sheridan Road at 8:27 p.m. on Sept. 4, police said. He was taken to Illinois Masonic Hospital, where he died three days later, according to the Cook County Medical Examiner’s office, which ruled his death a homicide.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox could reimagine amateur scouting process in the wake of Mike Shirley's resignation
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — White Sox general manager <b>Chris Getz</b> declined to comment on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/12/white-sox-amateur-scouting-director-mike-shirley-resigns-chris-getz-garrett-crochet-colson-montgomery-grant-taylor-jacob-gonzalez-hagen-smith-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>Saturday’s resignation of scouting director </u><b><u>Mike Shirely</u></b></a>, and the organization has termed the departure as “a personnel matter.” League sources confirmed to the Sun-Times that it came while Shirley was on administrative leave due to an internal investigation.</p><p>The future of Sox amateur scouting is a baseball matter under Getz’s purview. While he was willing to comment on it, the answers aren’t definitive yet. No one will be elevated to the amateur scouting position on an interim basis, and a meaningful outside hire could ultimately result. But Getz — who has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/07/white-sox-nearing-surprising-al-central-title-behind-remodeled-player-acquisition-process-chris-getz-josh-barfield-david-keller-miguel-vargas-tristan-peters-luis-castillo-curtis-mead-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>overseen pro scouting becoming a “spoke” in the larger wheel of the player acquisition department</u></a> — repeatedly suggested the amateur scouting operation Shirley ran was already in line to be restructured.</p><p>“We're looking at a lot of different ways and we’ve been doing that for a while — not just a clear restructure — of conducting business on that front,” Getz said. “Once that's mapped out, we'll figure out what the needs are for the organization.”</p><p>Especially with a decision as momentous as the first overall pick this past July, there are more cooks in the kitchen for White Sox drafts than just scouts, as mapping out a player development strategy has become a larger part of the equation. Getz said the Sox are reviewing their entire “player evaluation process,” but did not betray concern that the team needed to repair their organizational reputation on the scouting front after a New York Times report indicated concerns were raised about Shirley’s conduct at the Area Codes Games, an event well-attended by evaluators across MLB.</p><p>“We've got a really good group of people that are talented, and really love working here,” Getz said. “My job is to find pathways for us to get to good decisions.”</p><h3><b>Castillo going in ‘wrong direction’</b></h3><h3></h3><p><b>Luis Castillo</b> was a pitcher with a great career having a poor season when the White Sox acquired him on Aug. 2, but the team felt with more changeup use and some delivery tweaks, they could restore him to previous heights.</p><p>Instead, with Castillo sporting a 7.76 ERA in a Sox uniform and his velocity flagging to the low-90s in his last start, it’s gone in the other way.</p><p>“The quality of the pitches have definitely gone the wrong direction,” Getz said. “It has been surprising.”</p><p>Castillo is under contract through 2027 (with a 2028 vesting option), so the team is committed to finding a fix for his woes. But when it comes to restoring the 33-year-old to effectiveness in the final two weeks of this season, they’ve yet to say when Castillo’s next outing will be, or what form it will take.</p><p>“We're running out of time,” Getz said. “Big picture-wise, we've got some work to do.”</p><h3><b>Quero to play winter ball</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Having fallen out of the Sox catching rotation after entering last season as a top-100 prospect, <b>Edgar Quero</b> intends to play in the Dominican winter league (LIDOM) this offseason.</p><p>The 23-year-old Quero estimates he’ll play for 4-6 weeks, and while he hasn’t discussed the decision with the team yet, indications are they’ll support the idea. Quero acknowledged that in light of this season, his future role with the Sox is uncertain.</p><p>Quero believes he’s better than his .203/.284/.257 batting line in 69 games this season have shown.</p>

entries.title: WAR, what is it good for? Absolutely nothin’, if you’re Cubs starting pitchers: ‘I’ll take our guys any day’
entries.summary: <p>WAR, what is it good for?</p><p>If you’re a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> starting pitcher, you probably think the answer is “absolutely nothin’,” because the stat — wins above replacement, for the uninitiated, a popular evaluation metric — doesn’t think much of Cubs starting pitching.</p><p>Coming into Monday, the group had the fourth-lowest fWAR in baseball, at 5.1. Expand the evaluation to the Cubs’ pitching staff as a whole, including the fan-maddening bullpen, and they had the worst fWAR in baseball, at 4.1.</p><p>Back to the starting pitching, exclusively, the case against the stat being the end-all, be-all descriptor of quality gets plenty of backing from the teams in the Cubs’ company: The three spots in front of them were occupied by other playoff contenders in the Diamondbacks, White Sox and Padres, with the Astros one spot below.</p><p>As you might imagine, there are plenty willing to take that side of the argument inside the Cubs’ clubhouse.</p><p>“If you want to refer to a WAR metric or something like that, that metric is flawed in a lot of ways when it comes to starting pitchers,” Cubs lefty Matthew Boyd said Monday. “There’s so many ways to take a starting pitcher and to describe what kind of output they have.</p><p>“I’ll take our guys any day. We’re going to compete. If those mattered so much, they wouldn’t let you go compete when the time came.”</p><p>It’s true, umps don’t stop pitchers for a pre-outing WAR check.</p><p>But you don’t need to be a faceless math equation to harbor concerns about what Cubs starters are capable of come the postseason.</p><p>Just a couple weeks ago, team president Jed Hoyer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >cited the need for greater consistency from that group</a>, painting them as something of a question mark compared to the relative certainty of a position-player group that ranked Monday, by the same fWAR measure, as the sport’s top offensive and defensive team.</p><p>It’s hard to argue that the rotation has found that consistency, even though it’s not looking like a glaring weakness, either.</p><p>Boyd, for instance, is not finding the same level of success he did earlier in the summer. In his first seven starts after returning from the injured list in late June, he had a sparkling 1.93 ERA. In the eight starts since, he’s got a 5.18 ERA.</p><p>Righty Clay Holmes looked incredible for a stretch after arriving in a trade-deadline deal, Hoyer’s front office pushing in significant chips to bolster the rotation. Holmes gave up just one run across four outings, but in the two starts since, he allowed a career-worst eight runs to the Marlins and walked a season-high four batters against the Pirates, surrendering rare homers in both.</p><p>Righty Kevin Gausman, Hoyer’s other big deadline addition, has swung wildly between dominant performances and getting knocked around, that concern over inconsistency personified.</p><p>And while lefty Shota Imanaga has been mostly strong — especially lately, with three runs allowed in 12 innings over his last two outings — he’s cited a personal desire <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/05/cubs-shota-imanaga-craig-counsell-home-run-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" >to “build back trust”</a> after some poor starts. He still woke up Monday with more home runs allowed, 34, than any other pitcher in baseball.</p><p>These will be the pitchers the Cubs need to deliver in the playoffs if they’re going to accomplish the sky-high goals they’ve held all season.</p><p>Cubs starting pitchers might not look like much to the WAR-mongers. But they’re ready for that responsibility of the team’s October fate resting on their shoulders.</p><p>“This time of year and the playoffs, it’s exciting because you get to dictate it. It’s what you want, and as a starting group, we’re really excited about that,” Boyd said. “This is the time of the year that you dream about when you’re a starting pitcher. It’s the opportunity to lead your team to victory in important games, in meaningful games. We cherish that.</p><p>“You need a stable of starters in the playoffs. Teams that got there had that last year. Every year, they have that. There’s anomalies, but that’s the standard theme: Starting pitching gets you to where you want to go.</p><p>“These guys are awesome, and whenever our days [to take the ball] are, we’re excited to go forward and do what we can for this ballclub.”</p>

entries.title: Three things still at stake when the Sky return from the FIBA World Cup break
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> will return from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/olympic-sports/2026/09/13/us-womens-fiba-world-cup-title-france" >FIBA World Cup break</a> Sept. 17 to play the Mystics at home. They have only four regular-season games remaining and have already been eliminated from the playoffs.</p><p>So what’s at stake in the final stretch? Here are three things still hanging in the balance.</p><h3><b>1. Coach Tyler Marsh’s job</b></h3><h3></h3><p>It’s certainly possible that general manager Jeff Pagliocca has already made up his mind about Marsh, one way or the other. But if he’s still evaluating, securing a few more victories could go a long way toward bolstering Marsh’s case to return for a third season.</p><p>Picture the Sky sweeping their final four games. (You’ll really have to stretch your imagination here, given that their longest winning streak of the season is three games.) If they did it, though, they’d end the season with a record of 19-25.</p><p>That would mean Marsh nearly doubled his win total from his first season. It would mean the Sky beat six of the eight playoff teams. And it would demonstrate an impressive ability to keep the team motivated even after its playoff hopes flamed out.</p><p>Of course, a strong finish wouldn’t erase the games the Sky blew during the heart of the season, which derailed their chances of making the playoffs.</p><p>It may simply be too little, too late. Pagliocca <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/03/amid-losing-season-sky-gm-jeff-pagliocca-still-sees-playoff-potential-and-an-underrated-young-core" >has made it clear</a> throughout the season that he believes the roster was strong enough to make the playoffs, even with all the injuries, meaning Marsh may have to bear the responsibility for falling short.</p><h3><b>2. Course correction from the rookies</b></h3><h3></h3><p>There will be more minutes for the youngsters in the final stretch, according to Marsh, which should be good news for Gabriela Jaquez, the Sky’s No. 5 pick in the draft.</p><p>Jaquez came onto the scene hot, looking like an All-Rookie selection through her first 15 starts. Then she got buried in the rotation as veterans returned from injury, and she never quite looked like the same player. More minutes should give her a chance to prove that, with the right opportunity, she can be the scrappy, dynamic wing she appeared to be from the start.</p><p>Rookie Sydney Taylor should benefit from more minutes, too. Taylor, the Sky’s breakout star of the season, has struggled to find her stroke since suffering a groin injury and being placed on a minutes restriction. But she returned from the FIBA break feeling healthy, and Marsh thinks she’ll be able to handle something closer to her previous workload.</p><h3><b>3. Proving they can compete with the Mystics</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Marsh and Pagliocca have maintained all season that their young core of Taylor, Jaquez, Kamilla Cardoso and the injured Rickea Jackson is on par with the playoff-bound Mystics’.</p><p>They’ll have a chance to prove it at home on the 17th, and again on the road on the 24th.</p><p>The Mystics whomped the Sky the first time they met in May. The Sky were mired in a five-game losing streak and played disorganized, uninspired basketball. It was a troubling display of the divergent paths the two teams are on.</p><p>A year ago, the Sky and Mystics were in basically the same position: struggling teams with some promising young players. This year, the Mystics have completely turned things around. They are 24-16 and currently hold the No. 7 seed, while the Sky are once again on the outside looking in.</p><p>Are the Sky really just a few tweaks and turns away from joining the Mystics? Actually competing with them would lend some credibility to that idea.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/olympic-sports/2026/09/13/us-womens-fiba-world-cup-title-france" >U.S. wins women’s FIBA World Cup title, beating France 97-79</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Lawmakers name acting legislative inspector general after McCuskey resignation
entries.summary: <p>A former federal prosecutor who investigated crimes against humanity committed by Saddam Hussein will be tasked with probing allegations of misconduct by Illinois lawmakers beginning next month.</p><p>The bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission named David Risley acting legislative inspector general effective Oct. 1, taking the place of Michael McCuskey, who last week <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/09/08/mike-mccuskey-resigns-benton-report-investigation-complaint" target="_blank" ><u>announced his resignation</u></a> at the end of the month in the wake of complaints about his handling of sexual harassment allegations that have roiled Springfield.</p><p>Risley, who previously worked as an investigator under former Legislative Inspector General Carol Pope, was an assistant U.S. attorney for Illinois’ central district, and he served in the U.S. Regime Crimes Liaison Office investigating crimes against humanity in Iraq.</p><p>Risley is also a former ethics officer for the state Department of Transportation who has maintained a part-time adviser role in the inspector general's office, and he has hosted a podcast on crime and criminal justice policy since 2019, according to his professional website.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Springfield.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>McCuskey, a former federal judge, has held the post since 2022, but came under fire this summer for his investigation into former state Rep. Harry Benton, the Plainfield Democrat who stepped down in the wake of sexual harassment allegations.</p><p>McCuskey determined Benton broke state law by sexually harassing three women, including a lobbyist who later rebutted several “inaccuracies” in the inspector general’s report and said McCuskey didn’t take notes or record their interview.</p><p>The case separately raised questions about the judgment of Illinois House Speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>Emanuel “Chris” Welch</u></a>, who knew of allegations against Benton two years before those that led to the representative’s ouster, but still directed $1.4 million to his reelection campaign.</p><p>“The position of Legislative Inspector General is too important to sit vacant, especially in the context of the current moment,” Ethics Commission Chair state Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, said in a statement. “The public’s trust has understandably been shaken by recent events, which is why the Commission has acted swiftly to fill the position to provide a seamless transition. We are committed to ensuring the highest ethical standards are enforced and that all complainants, respondents and witnesses are given the due process and consideration they deserve."</p><p>Risley becomes the newest face of an office that has failed to rein in Springfield’s entrenched culture of harassment — largely because lawmakers haven’t given it the teeth to independently oversee the Capitol.</p><p>When she stepped down as legislative inspector general in 2021, Pope dismissed the post as “essentially a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/7/14/22578069/watchdog-legislative-inspector-general-carol-pope-ethics-reforms-illinois-legislature" target="_blank" ><u>paper tiger</u></a>” and declared “true ethics reform is not a priority” for lawmakers.</p><p>Ethics experts have long called for changes to state law to allow the legislative inspector general to issue subpoenas and publish reports without the approval of the ethics commission, which includes eight lawmakers.</p><p>Risley can serve until the current inspector general term ends in mid-2028, but the ethics commission is seeking applicants to take on the permanent role well before then.</p>

entries.title: Customs officer was offered free sex acts to stop gunpoint rapes, sex worker testifies
entries.summary: <p>Days into the trial of a<b> </b>federal immigration officer accused of several <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >“gunpoint sexual assaults,”</a><b> </b>jurors<b> </b>Monday<b> </b>finally heard the story behind a photo taken of the officer at a seafood buffet<b> </b>in Hoffman Estates.</p><p>A sex worker took the witness stand and explained how her boss in China had sent her to a 2022<b> </b>lunch<b> </b>meeting<b> </b>there<b> </b>with a mission and a message.</p><p>Her mission: Secure a photograph of U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer Luis Uribe. The message, she said, “was asking him not to harm our girls — and we agree to provide free sex to him once per week.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became ‘perfect mark’ for prostitution ring, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Still, that woman also admitted she’d lied in the past about who joined them at the<b> </b>lunch<b> </b>meeting, that she had failed to tell the feds about multiple encounters she’d had with Uribe,<b> </b>and that she never experienced any of the violence <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" target="_blank" >described by others</a> who testified against him.</p><p>“He never harmed me,”<b> </b>the woman testified.</p><p>Federal prosecutors say Uribe<b> </b>used his gun and badge to sexually assault four women in Schaumburg and Naperville in 2022,<b> </b>when he was assigned to O’Hare International Airport. They say his photo was taken at the northwest suburban buffet so it could be circulated among the community he’d targeted.</p><p>Michael Clancy, Uribe’s attorney, maintains his client was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" >set up by a prostitution ring</a> overseen by a boss in China. He acknowledged Uribe visited prostitutes and is a “flawed”<b> </b>human being — but he said there’s no proof that Uribe robbed and raped the women, as prosecutors allege.</p><p>The trial at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse appears to be nearing its end, with prosecutors likely to rest their case Tuesday. Uribe might then testify in his own defense.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" >In CBP officer’s rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: ‘He showed a badge’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Uribe is charged with 10 counts of deprivation of civil rights under color of law and one count of brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence. He has been held in federal custody since his arrest last December.</p><p>The woman who testified Monday has been described by Clancy as the “on-the-ground Chicago boss of a prostitution ring that is [run] by another boss, located in China.”<b> </b>But when asked by Clancy whether she was “the boss of a prostitution ring,”<b> </b>she denied it.</p><p>“I am never a boss,” she said. “I worked, myself.”</p><p>The woman said she was born in China and spoke little English. She testified Monday with help from an interpreter and became visibly frustrated at times.</p><p>She twice complained “my head hurts” while fielding the lawyers’ questions.</p><p>The woman explained she came to the Chicago area around 2018 or 2019, and first met Uribe at a Naperville<b> </b>Red Roof Inn. She said Uribe paid $300<b> </b>to have sex<b> </b>with her and another woman.<b> </b>Later, she said, Uribe told her he was “immigration police.”</p><p>She said they exchanged phone numbers and continued their relationship. She admitted Monday she had three<b> </b>or four additional encounters with Uribe after their meeting at the Red Roof Inn — encounters she’d never told federal authorities about.</p><p>“They didn’t ask me about that,” she insisted.</p><p>The woman said she used Google Translate<b> </b>to communicate with Uribe.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" >O’Hare-based Border Protection officer sexually abused, robbed women at gunpoint, indictment claims</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>She acknowledged once asking Uribe to run out and buy K-Y Jelly<b> </b>for her while she was working in Schaumburg. She also admitted becoming jealous<b> </b>when she saw Uribe touching a friend of hers.</p><p>Meanwhile, she said she thought Uribe might be able to help<b> </b>with her immigration status, as well as with a friend who’d been detained by immigration authorities.</p><p>“When he couldn’t help you and your bosses, you turned on him, correct?” Clancy asked her.</p><p>She denied it, insisting she only became angry when she saw Uribe touching her friend.</p><p>The woman also acknowledged she’d previously lied to cover up the fact that the same friend had attended the lunch<b> </b>meeting at the seafood buffet in Hoffman Estates. She said her friend, who was pregnant at the time, actually took the photo of Uribe that day.</p><p>“I only lied once,” the woman told the jury.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard<b> </b>Rothblatt<b> </b>questioned the woman about the lunch meeting. He asked multiple times<b> </b>whether Uribe denied harming anyone. The woman simply told Rothblatt, “that didn’t come up.”</p><p>But when the meeting was over, she said Uribe “followed us back to the hotel”<b> </b>and had sex with two other women.</p><p>“And did he pay for it?” Rothblatt asked.</p><p>“No,” she said. “It’s free.”</p>

entries.title: Un año después de operativo, Chicago celebra su fortaleza en el Desfile del Día de la Independencia de México
entries.summary: <p>Un año después de que las amenazas de inmigración atenuaran muchas de las celebraciones del Día de la Independencia de México en Chicago, el desfile de este año tenía como objetivo recuperar los 400,000 espectadores que esperaba reunir.</p><p>El desfile del año pasado <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/09/05/realizaran-desfile-del-dia-de-la-independencia-de-mexico-en-la-villita-a-pesar-de-las-amenazas-de-ice" target="_blank" >continuó como estaba planeado</a>, a pesar de los temores de redadas de inmigración durante el Operativo Midway Blitz, la campaña de control migratorio del presidente Donald Trump que tenía como objetivo Chicago. Sin embargo, los líderes alentaron a los asistentes potenciales a hacer lo que consideraran más seguro y a ver el desfile desde casa, si así lo deseaban.</p><p>Este año, el tema del 55.º evento anual fue "Unidos cabalgamos: Más fuertes que nunca". Organizado por la Cámara de Comercio de La Villita, los organizadores dijeron que el evento es uno de los desfiles más grandes del Medio Oeste y sirve como una celebración cultural y un motor económico para los negocios locales.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-838f2d" entries.title: City Council committee backs raising threshold for taking on future debt
entries.summary: <p>Over strenuous objections from Mayor Brandon Johnson’s most powerful ally, a City Council committee backed a measure Monday that would make it more difficult for Chicago to borrow money and increase the mountain of debt imposed on future generations of taxpayers.</p><p>Retiring Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/14/mayor-brandon-johnson-higher-borrowing-threshold" >initially wanted to raise</a> the threshold for approving city borrowing from a simple majority, or 26 votes, to a two-thirds majority, or 34 votes. That would have allowed 17 Council members to block future borrowing.</p><p>But Quinn lowered the bar to three-fifths, or 30 votes, hoping to appease colleagues and attract additional votes — and it worked. On Monday, the Finance Committee voted 21-9 to approve the revised ordinance.</p><p>It was the latest show of force by a renegade Council majority that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative city budget. </p><p>Budget Committee Chair Jason Ervin (28th) questioned the timing of the latest power play. It came a day after Johnson launched his re-election bid and just weeks before the mayor unveils his fourth, possibly final, city budget.</p><p>“Twenty-six votes is enough to pass any and every item that we do. And to allow a minority of members to effectively hold everybody hostage — I don’t think is in the best interest, not only of this city, but how democracy works,” Ervin told committee members.</p><p>“Why now? ... We need to look at the optics of how this will be perceived — especially in minority communities, as to what’s being done to whom, by whom.”</p><p>Senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee has similarly argued that allowing a minority to block “bond ordinances for critical infrastructure for whatever reason” would only “lead to gridlock and potentially harmful delays on critical investments that the city needs to make to preserve” roads, bridges and other aging infrastructure.</p><p>“Who knows what interests a super-minority might have, what political interests they might have at any given time to bring the city to a halt? You don’t want to create an opportunity for a super-minority to play politics with critical infrastructure that keeps the city going,” Lee has told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) countered that the higher borrowing threshold is “not about who the current mayor is. … This change applies to all future mayors.”</p><p>“This body has started to — and it’s refreshing — act independently of administrations and the executive, and by requiring the super-majority vote, it makes the dialogue and engagement with each of us more valuable,” Reilly said.</p><p>“When you need more votes to get debt issued, it requires very specific conversations with each of us. … Having more cooks in the kitchen to push back and ask tough questions to determine whether or not the amount of debt we’re issuing is prudent or in the taxpayers interest [is a good thing]. We want more scrutiny. We want more vetting.”</p><p>Last year, the Council almost blocked an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/18/830-million-bond-issue-city-borrowing-costs-backloaded-repayment-schedule" target="_blank" >$830 million general obligation bond issue </a>that included a back-loaded repayment schedule that raised the overall price tag to $2 billion.</p><p>Johnson’s 26-23 victory was secured only after the mayor had to cast the third tie-breaking vote of his tenure. That vote broke a 25-25 tie to kill Reilly’s attempt to postpone the vote.</p><p></p><p>"When we borrow, we are making a promise that future taxpayers and future City Councils are gonna be required to keep. And given our current debt burden, our pension obligations, the many fiscal challenges we have ahead of us, it's entirely reasonable that taking on of new debt should really require a higher level of consensus," said Downtown Ald. Bill Conway (34th), a former investment banker. </p><p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson was lukewarm about a two-thirds requirement, saying it “has some strengths and weaknesses.” But he supports a three-fifths threshold.</p><p>“Whether this is a long-term fix or just a temporary pumping of the brakes, it is necessary and probably sends a good signal to the rating agencies that we kind of get that we can’t continue the way that we’ve been going so, let’s slow it down,” Ferguson said.</p><p>Ferguson pointed to the negative outlook letter that Standard & Poor's issued recently about the Chicago Public Schools and how its financial crisis affects city finances.</p><p>“We're hurtling towards the edge — an edge where nobody knows where the tipping point is. One step above junk bond status. Yet what are we doing? We're proposing the issuing of more debt," Ferguson said. "This isn’t a political thing. This is math.”</p><p>According to the Civic Federation, the city’s outstanding net debt rose by 32.8%, from $22 billion to $29.2 billion, between 2014 and 2023 — an amount driven by increased O'Hare Airport debt that was retired by airline revenues.</p><p></p>
